edges.effect_quant: Pediatric and youth studies consistently show worse dry-eye symptom scores or tear-film metrics with heavier device exposure. A school-based cross-sectional study found significantly higher dry-eye risk above roughly 3 to 3.5 hours of daily device use, and a pediatric case-control study linked smartphone use with dry eye disease in children. Acute experimental evidence also shows that one hour of smartphone gaming worsens symptoms and sharply reduces blink rate in school-aged children.
edges.population: children, adolescents, and youth with prolonged daily digital screen exposure
edges.mechanism: Excessive screen use lowers blink rate, increases interblink interval, and can destabilize the tear film during sustained near work, which plausibly worsens ocular-surface discomfort and dry-eye symptoms.
edges.summary: The literature leans harmful here. Longer screen exposure in children and adolescents is associated with more dry-eye symptoms and worse tear-function markers, even if some of the evidence is observational rather than fully longitudinal.
edges.caveats: The evidence base is still somewhat mixed in design quality and includes cross-sectional and case-control work rather than large long-term cohorts. Device ergonomics, ambient humidity, and baseline ocular-surface health also influence symptom severity.
